items.title: 14.1.2 Concept of a Vector in Space

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.3 (Book# 14.1.3). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.2 here is the book's 14.1.3.

The set \(R^{3} = \{(x, y, z) : x, y, z \in R\}\) is called 3-dimensional space. An element \((x, y, z)\) of \(R^{3}\) represents a point \(P(x, y, z)\), which is uniquely determined by its coordinates \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). Given a vector \(\underline{u}\) in space, there exists a unique point \(P(x, y, z)\) in space such that the vector \(\underline{OP}\) is equal to \(\underline{u}\) (see figure). Now each element \((x, y, z) \in R^{3}\) is associated with a unique ordered triple \((x, y, z)\), which represents the vector

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Reading the set notation: \(R^{3} = \{(x, y, z) : x, y, z \in R\}\) means \"all triples \((x, y, z)\) whose three entries are real numbers\". \(R^{3}\) is just the name for space.
Why can every vector be written as \([x, y, z]\)? A vector may be drawn anywhere (only its length and direction matter). Slide it, without turning, until its tail sits at \(O\). Its head then lands at exactly one point \(P(x, y, z)\), and those three numbers describe the vector completely.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Point or vector? Round brackets \((x, y, z)\) name a point (a position); square brackets \([x, y, z]\) name a vector (a movement). The same three numbers can mean either: \(P(2, 3, 5)\) is a place, and \([2, 3, 5]\) is the move from \(O\) to that place.
Example: the vector from \((1, 1, 1)\) to \((3, 4, 6)\) moves \(3 - 1 = 2\), \(4 - 1 = 3\), \(6 - 1 = 5\), so it is \([2, 3, 5]\); slid to the origin it ends at \(P(2, 3, 5)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(R^{3}\) is the set of all ordered triples of real numbers: 3-dimensional space.
Every point \(P(x, y, z)\) has exactly one coordinate triple.
Every vector \(\underline{u}\) in space equals exactly one \(\underline{OP}\), so \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\).
Round brackets: point. Square brackets: vector.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Mixing up the point \(P(x, y, z)\) and the vector \([x, y, z]\); they share numbers but are different objects.
Thinking a vector must start at \(O\): only after sliding it there does its head give \([x, y, z]\).
